analysis.one_liner: Guaranteed health coverage for every American through regulated private plans, with subsidies paid for by new taxes.
analysis.headline: The Senate's version of the Clinton health care plan, introduced by the Majority Leader with zero cosponsors in August 1994, was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar but was never taken up by any committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required every health plan to accept all applicants regardless of health status, charge the same premium to everyone in a rating area, and cover a standard benefits package modeled on the plan federal employees get. It would have helped individuals and small employers pay premiums, added prescription drug coverage to Medicare, and financed it all through tobacco taxes, assessments on insurers and self-insured plans, a cap on the tax-free treatment of very generous employer benefits, and required employer premium payments. It was the Senate companion to President Clinton's health plan and died without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The uninsured and people with preexisting conditions, who would gain guaranteed, portable coverage that cannot be denied or priced based on health; low- and moderate-income families, who would get premium and cost-sharing assistance; small employers, who would receive subsidies to cover their workers; seniors, who would gain Medicare coverage of outpatient prescription drugs; and people needing long-term care, who would get a voluntary public nursing home insurance program plus strict standards for long-term care policies. Rural and underserved communities would gain through essential community provider rules, community health centers, and full funding for WIC.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured Americans and people with preexisting conditions

how_it_helps.text: Ends health-based discrimination in insurance: no plan could deny coverage, impose waiting periods, or charge higher premiums based on medical history, and no one could be dropped for getting sick except for fraud or nonpayment.

Guarantees a standard benefits package for everyone, with actuarial value equal to the Blue Cross/Blue Shield standard option federal employees receive — including hospital care, prescription drugs, mental health and substance abuse services, preventive care, and dental and vision care for children.
Requires states to run premium and cost-sharing assistance programs for people who cannot afford coverage, and provides subsidies to small employers that provide or expand coverage for their workers.
Adds Medicare coverage of outpatient prescription drugs, with manufacturers required to pay rebates to the government on covered drugs.

Creates a voluntary public insurance program for nursing home care (coverage capped at $90,000) and imposes federal standards on the long-term care insurance market, which had been notorious for misleading sales practices.

Finances the expansion through increased tobacco excise taxes, assessments on insured and self-insured health plans, a 25% tax on high-cost community-rated plans, and limits on the tax-free treatment of the most generous employer health benefits — rather than adding a new burden on the uninsured.

Guarantees health plans must contract with certified essential community providers such as community health centers, rural clinics, public hospitals, and mental health providers, so safety-net providers are not excluded from the new system; also fully funds WIC.
Repeals the health insurance industry's exemption from federal antitrust law, letting the Sherman and Clayton Acts apply to health insurance.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of 25 or more workers (and smaller employers that elect in) would have to pay premiums toward their employees' coverage, though small employers get subsidies. Everyone would pay somewhat more through higher tobacco taxes, assessments on insured and self-insured health plans that get passed into premiums, and the eventual taxation of employer health benefits beyond a permitted level starting in 2004. Medicare beneficiaries would face new copayments on lab tests and home health services, and workers with very rich employer plans would lose part of their tax break. Every citizen and lawful resident would be required to enroll in coverage and pay their share of premiums.

drawbacks.text: Nearly every employer would face a new obligation to pay premiums toward workers' coverage, and employers with self-insured plans would pay a new monthly assessment — a genuine cost that employer groups fought.

Beginning in 2004, employer health benefits beyond the permitted level would be counted as taxable income to employees, shrinking a tax break that many middle- and upper-income workers with generous plans relied on.
The bill requires every citizen and lawful resident to enroll in a health plan and pay premiums, a mandate that falls on individuals regardless of whether they feel they need coverage.

It would create a heavy administrative structure — a National Health Benefits Board, purchasing cooperatives in every rating area, quality and fraud councils, and deficit-control commissions — whose complexity was itself a political liability and a real implementation risk.

It pays for itself partly by cutting Medicare payments to hospitals and teaching programs and by imposing new copayments on Medicare lab tests and home health services, shifting some costs onto beneficiaries and providers.

Its deficit-control title could automatically reduce premium assistance and other subsidies in later years if health costs grew beyond the set baseline, meaning the help for working families was not fully guaranteed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Weighed honestly, this was the largest proposed expansion of health security since Medicare: guaranteed coverage that cannot be taken away for getting sick, prescription drugs under Medicare, and income-based help with premiums. The costs were real — an employer mandate, new assessments and tobacco taxes, taxation of the most generous employer benefits, an individual mandate, and a bureaucracy most observers considered overly complex — and the political system ultimately judged the package too big and too complicated to pass. But the costs in the bill were spread across employers, smokers, health plans, and high-benefit workers, while the benefits concentrated on the people the existing system priced out; the alternative that prevailed was the status quo, whose costs fall on the uninsured themselves.

outcome.mechanism: The Majority Leader introduced it with no cosponsors in the last five months of the Congress; the Senate read it twice and put it on the calendar, but no committee ever considered it and it never came to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senate Majority Leader George Mitchell introduced the Health Security Act on August 3, 1994, as the lone sponsor, with introductory remarks entered in the Record.

On August 5, 1994, the bill was read a second time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 542) — the list of bills eligible for floor action — but it never received a hearing, a committee markup, or a floor vote.

The 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, with the bill still sitting on the calendar and every provision, including universal coverage, Medicare drug coverage, and its financing taxes, expiring with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of the health care overhaul came out ahead: insurers kept their ability to price and deny coverage by health status, large employers avoided the premium mandate and assessments, tobacco companies avoided the tax increase, and workers with generous health plans kept their full tax break. The uninsured, who the bill was written for, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, large employers, and tobacco companies

for.name: George J. Mitchell
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill on the Senate floor, delivered introductory remarks, and had it read twice and placed on the legislative calendar in an attempt to force a path to a vote before the session ended.

for.name: Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Proposed the Health Security Act the previous year and pressed Congress to pass comprehensive health reform; the Senate bill was the vehicle carrying his plan.

against.name: Bob Dole
against.what_they_did: Led the Senate Republican caucus, including a letter signed by 44 Republican senators pledging to block the bill from coming to a final vote, ensuring it never reached the floor.

against.name: Health insurance industry, led by the Health Insurance Association of America
against.what_they_did: Funded the 'Harry and Louise' television ad campaign criticizing the plan's mandated structure and ran a nationwide lobbying effort against guaranteed-issue and community-rating rules.

against.name: Daniel Patrick Moynihan
against.what_they_did: Distanced himself from the comprehensive plan and never brought it up in the Finance Committee, which held jurisdiction over the bill's tax and financing titles; no committee action ever occurred.

against.name: Small business groups, led by the National Federation of Independent Business
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the employer premium mandate that the bill imposed on businesses to help pay for workers' coverage.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held on the bill; the broader fight split largely by party, with all 44 Senate Republicans signing a pledge to block the bill, while several Democrats, including the Finance Committee chairman, also withheld support.

industries.note: The bill would have made every health plan accept all applicants at community-rated premiums and certified them against a standard benefits package, ending the industry's core business of underwriting by health status; in exchange it guaranteed a huge pool of mandated, partly subsidized customers through private plans. The industry fought it, and its defeat preserved the existing ability to deny or price coverage based on medical history.

Employers would owe premium payments toward workers' coverage and new assessments on self-insured plans, and the most generous employee health benefits would lose their tax-free status starting in 2004; firms with more than 500 workers could, however, keep running their own experience-rated plans outside the purchasing cooperatives.

The bill raised excise taxes on cigarettes and other tobacco products and imposed a new tax on roll-your-own tobacco, making tobacco users a principal funding source for coverage expansion. Its defeat preserved the lower tax rates.

Medicare coverage of outpatient prescription drugs would have created a large new paying market, but manufacturers would have had to pay rebates to the government on covered drugs, cutting into price levels. The bill's death delayed Medicare drug coverage by nearly a decade.

industries.industry: Academic health centers and teaching hospitals
industries.note: The bill created a dedicated trust fund with federal formula payments for graduate medical education and academic health centers and continued payments to medical, nursing, and dental schools. These subsidies died with the bill.

industries.industry: Blue Cross and Blue Shield plans
industries.note: The bill repealed the special federal tax rules for Blue Cross and Blue Shield organizations and subjected health insurance to federal antitrust law, ending preferential treatment those plans had long enjoyed.
